messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi is a 30-year-old curriculum designer who was referred by his primary care physician after reporting persistent sleep difficulties and a growing sense of detachment from his own life. He describes the traumatic event with a flat, careful precision that seems to hold his emotions at arm’s length. Eighteen months ago, he was in a relationship with a man named Marcus, a charismatic but volatile partner. One evening, after Marcus had been drinking heavily—the sharp, sweet smell of bourbon thick between them—an argument escalated. Kofi remembers Marcus’s hand connecting with his jaw, the crack of his head against the kitchen counter, and then the fall. He lay on the linoleum floor, the smell of something burning from a forgotten pan on the stove mixing with the bourbon, while Marcus stood over him, shouting. The physical pain in his ribs and jaw was immediate, but what lodged itself deeper was the terror—a raw, animal certainty that he might not get up.

In the months that followed, Kofi tried to move on. He threw himself into his work, designing inclusive educational modules for a public school district. But the world had become a minefield. A colleague’s offhand comment about a family dinner—*“Your mom must be so proud”*—would land with a sickening thud, and suddenly he would be back on that kitchen floor. The memory would arrive not as a picture, but as a full-body event: the phantom ache in his jaw, the smell of bourbon and burnt food flooding his nostrils, and the same visceral terror gripping his chest. He found that these memories did not just happen to him; they actively reshaped his sense of self. He began to feel that the person he had become—jumpy, withdrawn, unable to trust a kind word—was unrecognisable to the man he had been before. The injustice of it, the fact that Marcus had apologized and Kofi had never pressed charges, curdled into a quiet, pervasive bitterness. He started to feel dirty, as though the event had left a stain on his skin that no shower could wash away.

Kofi’s avoidance became a quiet architecture of his daily life. He stopped going to bars or restaurants that might serve alcohol, the mere whiff of beer on a passerby’s breath enough to trigger a cascade of physical memory. He began to dread family gatherings, because any comment about family felt like a pointed reminder of the home he had shared with Marcus. The more he avoided, the more the memories seemed to stalk him. He noticed that the memories themselves were becoming triggers: a sudden flash of the terror would leave him scanning his environment for danger, and a lingering phantom smell would send him checking the stove at home, even when nothing was on. This cycle tightened over months. At work, he found himself snapping at a colleague who had left a candle burning in the break room; the burnt-wax smell sent him into a cold sweat, and he had to excuse himself to the bathroom to wash his hands repeatedly, trying to scrub away the feeling of contamination.

The weight of his unrecognisable self bore down hardest on his career. A curriculum designer needs to collaborate, to facilitate workshops, to share meals with colleagues. Kofi now ate lunch alone in his car, the doors locked, just to avoid the cafeteria’s mix of cooking smells and the casual conversations that might touch on family. His performance reviews noted a drop in collaborative spirit, and he began to fear he was being edged toward a performance improvement plan. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment of quiet horror: he had flinched—violently, visibly—when a friend placed a hand on his shoulder to get his attention. The friend’s face had crumpled with hurt, and Kofi had been unable to explain why he had reacted that way. He is seeking therapy now because he is afraid that the person he has become is permanent, and that the life he built—his career, his friendships—is dissolving around him. What frightens him most is the thought that the man on that kitchen floor was the real him all along, and that the person he thought he was had only ever been a fragile, temporary fiction.
